chapters.title: Act I, Scene 1 — Athens. A Room in the Palace of Theseus
paragraphs: [Enter Theseus, Hippolyta, Philostrate and Attendants.]

THESEUS. Now, beautiful Hippolyta, our wedding day is almost here. Four happy days will bring the next new moon. But oh, how slowly this old moon fades! It drags out my longing like a stepmother or a widow slowly spending a young man's inheritance.

HIPPOLYTA. Four days will quickly dissolve into night. Four nights will quickly pass in dreams. And then a new moon, curved like a silver bow freshly strung in the sky, will look down on our wedding celebration.

THESEUS. Go, Philostrate. Get the young people of Athens excited for festivities. Wake up the lively spirit of fun and celebration. Send melancholy off to funerals — that gloomy companion has no place at our party.
[Exit Philostrate.]
THESEUS. Hippolyta, I won your heart through battle, and courted you by defeating you in war. But I will marry you in a different way — with ceremony, with celebration, and with joy.
[Enter Egeus, Hermia, Lysander and Demetrius.]
EGEUS. All happiness to Theseus, our famous Duke!
THESEUS. Thank you, Egeus. What's your news?

EGEUS. I come full of frustration, with a complaint against my daughter Hermia. Step forward, Demetrius. My noble lord, this man has my permission to marry her. Step forward, Lysander. And, my gracious Duke, this man has bewitched my daughter's heart. You, Lysander, you have given her love poems and exchanged tokens of affection with my child. You have serenaded her by moonlight at her window with a pretend voice singing fake love songs. You have stolen her imagination with bracelets made of your hair, rings, trinkets, knickknacks, little gifts, flowers, and sweets — all powerful tools of persuasion on impressionable youth. With your cunning, you have stolen my daughter's heart and turned the obedience she owes me into stubborn defiance. And so, my gracious Duke, if she will not agree here before your grace to marry Demetrius, I invoke the ancient law of Athens: since she is mine, I may do with her as I choose. She will either marry this gentleman or face death, as the law directly provides.

THESEUS. What do you say, Hermia? Think carefully, young lady. You should regard your father as a god — the one who created your beauty, and to whom you are like a figure in wax that he printed and has the power to keep or destroy. Demetrius is a worthy gentleman.
HERMIA. So is Lysander.
THESEUS. He is, in his own right. But without your father's approval in this matter, Demetrius must be considered the worthier choice.
HERMIA. I wish my father could see things through my eyes.
THESEUS. It is rather your eyes that must see things through his judgment.

HERMIA. I beg your Grace to forgive me. I don't know what makes me bold enough, or whether it is proper for a modest young woman in such company to argue her case. But I beg your Grace to tell me the worst that could happen to me if I refuse to marry Demetrius.

THESEUS. Either death, or giving up the company of men forever. So think carefully about what you want, Hermia. Consider your youth, examine your feelings honestly. If you won't accept your father's choice, can you endure becoming a nun — locked away forever in a shadowy convent, living a childless life as a sister, chanting quiet hymns to the cold, barren moon? Those who can master their passions enough for that life are truly blessed. But the rose that is picked and used is happier in this world than the one that withers on the thorn and grows, lives, and dies in lonely virtue.
HERMIA. Then I will grow, live, and die that way, my lord, before I will hand over my freedom to a man whose unwanted control my soul refuses to accept.

THESEUS. Take time to think about it. By the next new moon — which is the day my love and I will be bound together in eternal partnership — on that day, you must either prepare to die for disobeying your father, or agree to marry Demetrius as he wishes, or swear on Diana's altar to live a life of celibacy forever.
DEMETRIUS. Give in, sweet Hermia. And Lysander, give up your wild claim to what is rightfully mine.
LYSANDER. You have her father's love, Demetrius. Let me have Hermia's. Why don't you marry him?
EGEUS. That's right, scornful Lysander — he does have my love. And what is mine, my love will give to him. She is mine, and I hand over all my rights to her to Demetrius.

LYSANDER. My lord, my family is just as good as his. I am just as wealthy. My love for her is greater than his. My prospects are in every way at least as good as Demetrius's, if not better. And on top of all that, beautiful Hermia loves me. So why shouldn't I press my claim? Demetrius — and I'll say it to his face — courted Nedar's daughter, Helena, and won her heart. And she, sweet lady, is devoted to him — hopelessly, obsessively devoted to this unfaithful, unreliable man.

THESEUS. I have to admit I've heard as much, and I meant to talk to Demetrius about it. But I was so caught up in my own affairs that it slipped my mind. But come, Demetrius, and you too, Egeus — you will both come with me. I have some private words for both of you. As for you, Hermia, prepare yourself to accept your father's wishes, or else the law of Athens — which we cannot bend — delivers you to death or to a vow of single life. Come, my Hippolyta. What's the matter, my love? Demetrius and Egeus, come along. I need to put you to work on some business related to our wedding, and discuss something with you that closely concerns you both.
EGEUS. We follow you with both duty and eagerness.
[Exeunt all but Lysander and Hermia.]
LYSANDER. What's wrong, my love? Why are you so pale? Why are the roses in your cheeks fading so fast?
HERMIA. Probably because they need rain — which I could easily give them from the storm of tears in my eyes.
LYSANDER. Oh, from everything I've ever read or heard in stories or history, the course of true love never ran smooth. Either the lovers were from different social classes —
HERMIA. Oh, how awful! Too high-born to be bound to someone low.
LYSANDER. Or they were mismatched in age —
HERMIA. Oh, how terrible! Too old to be engaged to someone young.
LYSANDER. Or the choice depended on family and friends —
HERMIA. Oh, hell! To have your love chosen by someone else's eyes!

LYSANDER. Or even when two people chose each other freely, war, death, or sickness attacked their love, making it last only a moment — swift as a shadow, short as any dream, brief as a flash of lightning on a dark night that lights up both heaven and earth in an instant, and before anyone can even say "Look!" the jaws of darkness swallow it up. That's how quickly bright things end in chaos.

HERMIA. If true lovers have always been crossed like this, then it must be fate's decree. So let us face our trial with patience, since it's as much a part of love as thoughts and dreams and sighs, wishes and tears — the faithful followers of love.

LYSANDER. Good thinking. So hear me out, Hermia. I have a widowed aunt, a wealthy woman with no children. Her home is about twenty miles from Athens, and she treats me like her only son. There, sweet Hermia, I can marry you — and the harsh Athenian law can't reach us there. If you love me, sneak out of your father's house tomorrow night. In the forest, about a mile outside of town — where I once met you with Helena to celebrate May Day — I'll wait for you there.

HERMIA. My dear Lysander! I swear to you by Cupid's strongest bow, by his best golden arrow, by the innocence of Venus's doves, by everything that binds souls together and makes love flourish, and by the fire that burned Queen Dido when the unfaithful Trojan Aeneas sailed away, and by all the promises men have ever broken — which outnumber all the promises women have ever made — in that very place you've named, tomorrow I will truly meet you there.
LYSANDER. Keep your promise, love. Look, here comes Helena.
[Enter Helena.]
HERMIA. Hello, Helena! Where are you off to?

HELENA. Did you call me beautiful? Take that back. Demetrius loves your beauty. Oh, lucky you! Your eyes are like guiding stars, and your voice is sweeter than a lark singing to a shepherd's ear when the wheat is green and the hawthorn is budding. If only beauty were as catching as sickness — I'd catch yours, Hermia, before I left. My ear would catch your voice, my eye your look, my tongue your sweet way of speaking. If the world were mine, except for Demetrius, I'd give up all the rest to be transformed into you. Oh, teach me how you look the way you do, and what magic you use to control Demetrius's heart!
HERMIA. I frown at him, and he still loves me.
HELENA. If only your frowns could teach my smiles that trick!
HERMIA. I curse him, and he gives me love.
HELENA. If only my prayers could inspire that kind of devotion!
HERMIA. The more I hate him, the more he follows me.
HELENA. The more I love him, the more he hates me.
HERMIA. His foolishness, Helena, isn't my fault.
HELENA. No, it's your beauty's fault. I wish that fault were mine!

HERMIA. Don't worry — he won't see my face anymore. Lysander and I are running away from this place. Before I met Lysander, Athens seemed like paradise to me. Oh, what power does my love have, that he has turned a heaven into a hell!

LYSANDER. Helena, we'll share our plans with you. Tomorrow night, when the moon reflects her silver face in the water, decorating the grass with drops of dew like liquid pearls — a time that always hides lovers' secret escapes — we plan to slip through the gates of Athens.

HERMIA. And in the forest where you and I used to lie on beds of pale primroses, sharing our secrets with each other — there Lysander and I will meet. And from there we'll turn our eyes away from Athens to find new friends and new companions. Goodbye, dear friend. Pray for us, and may good luck bring you your Demetrius! Keep your word, Lysander. We must deny ourselves the sight of each other until tomorrow at midnight.
LYSANDER. I will, my Hermia.
[Exit Hermia.]
LYSANDER. Goodbye, Helena. May Demetrius come to love you as much as you love him!
[Exit Lysander.]

HELENA. How is it that some people are so much happier than others? Everyone in Athens thinks I'm just as beautiful as Hermia. But what does that matter? Demetrius doesn't think so. He refuses to see what everyone else can see. And just as he makes a mistake by obsessing over Hermia's eyes, so do I by admiring his qualities. Love can take things that are ugly and worthless and transform them into something beautiful and dignified. Love doesn't see with the eyes but with the imagination — and that's why Cupid is always painted blind. And love has no taste for good judgment at all. Wings but no eyes represent its reckless haste. And that's why people say love is like a child, because it's so often fooled in its choices. Just as mischievous boys break their promises in games, the boy-god Love breaks his promises everywhere. Before Demetrius ever looked at Hermia, he swore oath after oath that he belonged only to me. But when he felt some warmth from Hermia, those oaths melted away like hail in sunshine. I'm going to tell him about Hermia's plan to run away. Then he'll chase after her through the forest tomorrow night. And if I get any thanks for this information, it will have cost me dearly. But this way, at least I'll get to see him when he goes there and comes back.
[Exit Helena.]

chapters.title: Act I, Scene 2 — The Same. A Room in a Cottage
paragraphs: [Enter Quince, Snug, Bottom, Flute, Snout  and Starveling.]
QUINCE. Is everyone here?
BOTTOM. The best thing to do would be to call them one by one, man by man, according to the list.
QUINCE. Here is the list of every man's name who has been chosen from all of Athens to act in our play for the Duke and Duchess on his wedding night.
BOTTOM. First, Peter Quince, tell us what the play is about. Then read the names of the actors. And then get to the point.
QUINCE. Well, our play is called _The Most Lamentable Comedy and Most Cruel Death of Pyramus and Thisbe_.
BOTTOM. An excellent piece of work, I can assure you, and a funny one too. Now, Peter Quince, call out the actors from the list. Everyone, spread out.
QUINCE. Answer when I call your name. Nick Bottom, the weaver.
BOTTOM. Here. Tell me what part I'm playing, and let's move on.
QUINCE. You, Nick Bottom, are assigned the role of Pyramus.
BOTTOM. What is Pyramus — a lover or a tyrant?
QUINCE. A lover, who kills himself very nobly for love.

BOTTOM. That'll require some tears if it's done properly. If I play the part, the audience had better have their handkerchiefs ready. I'll create a storm of emotion. I'll weep and wail to a certain degree. As for the rest — my real talent is for playing a tyrant. I could play Hercules brilliantly, or any part that tears the place apart. The raging rocks and shivering shocks shall break the locks of prison gates, and the sun god's chariot shall shine from far and make and wreck the foolish Fates. That was powerful stuff. Now name the rest of the actors. That was the Hercules style — a tyrant's style. A lover is more weepy.
QUINCE. Francis Flute, the bellows-mender.
FLUTE. Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE. Flute, you have to play Thisbe.
FLUTE. What is Thisbe? A wandering knight?
QUINCE. It's the lady that Pyramus has to fall in love with.
FLUTE. Oh no, please don't make me play a woman. I'm starting to grow a beard.
QUINCE. That doesn't matter. You'll play it in a mask, and you can make your voice as high as you want.
BOTTOM. If I can hide my face, let me play Thisbe too! I'll speak in an absurdly high little voice: "Thisne, Thisne!" — "Ah, Pyramus, my dear lover! Your dear Thisbe! And dear lady!"
QUINCE. No, no — you have to play Pyramus. And Flute, you're Thisbe.
BOTTOM. Fine, go on.
QUINCE. Robin Starveling, the tailor.
STARVELING. Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE. Robin Starveling, you'll play Thisbe's mother. Tom Snout, the tinker.
SNOUT. Here, Peter Quince.
QUINCE. You'll play Pyramus's father. I'll play Thisbe's father. Snug the joiner — you get the lion's part. And I think we have a complete cast.
SNUG. Do you have the lion's part written out? Please give it to me if you do, because I'm a slow learner.
QUINCE. You can improvise it — all you have to do is roar.
BOTTOM. Let me play the lion too! I'll roar so well it'll do any man's heart good to hear it. I'll roar so well the Duke will say, "Let him roar again! Let him roar again!"
QUINCE. If you roar too fiercely, you'll scare the Duchess and the ladies so badly they'll scream — and that would be enough to get us all hanged.
ALL. That would get every last one of us hanged.

BOTTOM. I'll grant you, friends, if you scare the ladies out of their wits, they'd have no choice but to hang us. But I'll modify my voice so that I roar as gently as a baby dove. I'll roar as sweetly as a nightingale.

QUINCE. You can't play any part except Pyramus. Pyramus is a handsome man — as fine a man as you'd see on a summer's day — a most charming, gentlemanly man. That's why you absolutely must play Pyramus.
BOTTOM. All right, I'll take it on. What kind of beard should I wear for the part?
QUINCE. Whatever you like.
BOTTOM. I'll perform it with either a straw-colored beard, an orange-tan beard, a deep purple-red beard, or a French-crown-gold beard — a perfect yellow.

QUINCE. Some of those French crowns have no hair at all, so then you'd play it bare-faced. But listen, everyone — here are your parts, and I beg you, request you, and urge you to memorize them by tomorrow night. Meet me in the woods outside town, about a mile out, by moonlight. That's where we'll rehearse. If we meet in the city, we'll be followed by nosy people, and our plans will be discovered. In the meantime, I'll make a list of the props we need for our play. Please don't let me down.
BOTTOM. We'll meet there, and we can rehearse freely and boldly. Work hard, learn your lines perfectly. Goodbye!
QUINCE. We meet at the Duke's oak tree.
BOTTOM. Good enough. Be there or face the consequences.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 1 — A Wood near Athens
paragraphs: [Enter a Fairy at one door, and Puck at another.]
PUCK. Hey there, spirit! Where are you wandering?

FAIRY. Over hills, over valleys, through bushes, through thorns, over parks, over fences, through floods, through fires — I wander everywhere, faster than the moon moves through the sky. I serve the Fairy Queen, scattering dew on the fairy rings in the grass. The tall cowslips are her bodyguards. You can see the gold spots on their petals — those are rubies, fairy gifts, and their freckles hold their fragrance. I have to go find some dewdrops here, and hang a pearl in every cowslip's ear. Goodbye, you big clumsy spirit — I have to go. Our Queen and all her fairies will be here any moment.

PUCK. The King is holding his celebrations here tonight. Make sure the Queen doesn't come near him. Oberon is furious because she has a lovely boy as her attendant — stolen from an Indian king. She's never had such a sweet child in her care. Jealous Oberon wants the boy to be one of his knights, to roam the wild forests with him. But she refuses to give up the beloved boy. She crowns him with flowers and makes him her entire joy. And now whenever they meet — in a grove or a meadow, by a clear fountain or under the sparkling starlight — they fight. Their arguments are so bad that all their fairies hide in acorn cups out of fear.

FAIRY. Unless I'm completely wrong about your appearance, you must be that mischievous and tricky spirit called Robin Goodfellow. Aren't you the one who frightens the village girls, skims the cream off the milk, sometimes messes with the grain mill, makes the breathless housewife churn butter for nothing, sometimes keeps the beer from fermenting properly, and leads nighttime travelers astray, laughing at their misfortune? The ones who call you Hobgoblin and sweet Puck — you do their work for them, and they have good luck. Aren't you him?

PUCK. You've got it right. I am that merry wanderer of the night. I perform tricks for Oberon and make him laugh. I fool a fat, well-fed horse by neighing like a young filly. Sometimes I lurk at the bottom of a gossip's drinking bowl disguised as a baked apple, and when she takes a sip, I bob up against her lips and pour the ale all down her wrinkled chin. The wisest old aunt, telling the saddest story, sometimes mistakes me for a three-legged stool. Then I slip out from under her, and down she tumbles, crying "Ow, my backside!" She falls into a coughing fit, and then all the others hold their sides and howl with laughter and sneeze and swear they've never had a funnier time. But make room, fairy — here comes Oberon.
FAIRY. And here comes my mistress. I wish he would go away!
[Enter Oberon at one door, with his Train, and Titania at another, with hers.]
OBERON. What bad luck, running into you by moonlight, proud Titania.
TITANIA. What? Jealous Oberon! Fairies, let's go. I've sworn off his bed and his company.
OBERON. Wait, reckless woman. Am I not your husband?

TITANIA. Then I must be your wife. But I know perfectly well that you've been sneaking away from fairyland, disguising yourself as a shepherd named Corin and sitting around all day playing flutes and writing love poems to some girl named Phillida. And why are you here now? You've come all the way from the farthest reaches of India just because that bouncing Amazon warrior woman, your boot-wearing mistress and warrior girlfriend, is about to marry Theseus — and you've come to bless their marriage bed.

OBERON. How can you shame me like this, Titania, bringing up Hippolyta — when I know about your love for Theseus? Didn't you lead him through the dark night away from Perigenia, whom he had taken by force? And didn't you make him break his promises to Aegles, Ariadne, and Antiopa?

TITANIA. These are all lies invented by jealousy. Ever since midsummer began, every time we've met — on a hill, in a valley, in a forest, in a meadow, by a paved fountain, by a stream edged with rushes, or on the sandy shore of the sea — to dance our fairy circles to the whistling wind, your brawling has ruined our fun. So the winds, having piped their music to us for nothing, have sucked up poisonous fogs from the sea in revenge. These fogs have fallen on the land and made every little river overflow its banks. The ox has strained at his plow for nothing. The farmer has wasted his sweat. The green grain has rotted before it could ripen. The sheep pens stand empty in the flooded fields, and the crows are fattened on the diseased flocks. The outdoor game-boards are filled with mud, and the intricate maze-paths in the grass are impossible to make out because nobody walks them anymore. People are confused about the seasons — they don't know if it's winter or not. No night is blessed with hymns or carols anymore. So the moon, ruler of the tides, pale with anger, fills the air with dampness, and diseases spread. Because of all this chaos, the seasons have gone haywire: frost falls on fresh red roses, and on old Winter's thin, icy head, a garland of sweet summer flowers sits as if in mockery. Spring, summer, fertile autumn, and angry winter have all swapped their usual appearances. The confused world can no longer tell which is which. And this whole crop of disasters comes from our quarrel, from our disagreement. We are their parents and their cause.
OBERON. Then fix it. It's up to you. Why would Titania defy her Oberon? All I'm asking for is the little changeling boy to be my attendant.

TITANIA. Put that idea out of your mind. All of fairyland couldn't buy that child from me. His mother was a follower of mine, and in the spice-scented Indian air, by night, she often sat beside me and gossiped. We would sit together on the golden sands of the shore, watching the merchant ships on the waves. We laughed to see the sails swell up, growing big-bellied with the playful wind. She — with her graceful, waddling walk, her womb already big with my young attendant — would imitate the ships, pretending to sail across the land to fetch me little presents, and then come back as if from a voyage, loaded with gifts. But she was mortal, and she died giving birth to that boy. For her sake I'm raising him, and for her sake I will not give him up.
OBERON. How long do you intend to stay in this forest?

TITANIA. Perhaps until after Theseus's wedding day. If you want to join peacefully in our dances and watch our moonlight celebrations, come with us. If not, stay away from me, and I'll stay away from you.
OBERON. Give me that boy, and I'll come with you.
TITANIA. Not for your entire fairy kingdom. Fairies, let's go! We'll end up in a real fight if I stay any longer.
[Exit Titania with her Train.]

OBERON. Fine, go. But you won't leave this forest until I've punished you for this insult. Come here, my gentle Puck. Do you remember the time I sat on a cliff overlooking the sea and heard a mermaid riding on a dolphin's back, singing such sweet and beautiful music that the rough sea grew calm at her song, and certain stars shot wildly from their orbits just to hear her?
PUCK. I remember.

OBERON. At that very moment I saw — though you couldn't — Cupid himself, fully armed, flying between the cold moon and the earth. He took careful aim at a beautiful, royal maiden seated in the west, and he shot his love-arrow sharply from his bow as if to pierce a hundred thousand hearts. But I watched as young Cupid's fiery arrow was quenched by the pure, cold moonbeams, and the royal maiden passed on untouched, lost in innocent thoughts, free from love. But I noticed where Cupid's arrow fell: it landed on a little western flower that was white as milk before, but turned purple from love's wound. Young girls call it love-in-idleness. Fetch me that flower — the herb I showed you once. Its juice, squeezed onto sleeping eyelids, will make any man or woman fall madly in love with the next living creature they see. Bring me this herb, and return before a whale can swim three miles.
PUCK. I'll circle the entire earth in forty minutes.
[Exit Puck.]

OBERON. Once I have this juice, I'll watch for Titania to fall asleep and drop the liquid into her eyes. The next thing she looks at when she wakes — whether it's a lion, bear, wolf, bull, meddling monkey, or busy ape — she'll pursue it with the intensity of passionate love. And before I remove the spell from her eyes — which I can do with another herb — I'll make her hand over the boy to me. But who's coming? I'll make myself invisible and listen in on their conversation.
[Enter Demetrius, Helena following him.]

DEMETRIUS. I don't love you, so stop following me. Where are Lysander and Hermia? I want to kill one of them, and the other is killing me. You told me they'd run off into this forest, and here I am, going mad in this forest because I can't find Hermia. Get out of here and stop following me.
HELENA. You attract me to you, you hard-hearted magnet — but what you attract isn't iron, because my heart is true as steel. Give up your power to draw me in, and I'll lose the power to follow you.
DEMETRIUS. Am I leading you on? Am I being sweet to you? Or am I not telling you in the plainest possible terms that I do not and cannot love you?

HELENA. And that's exactly why I love you even more. I'm like your dog, Demetrius. The more you beat me, the more I'll be devoted to you. Treat me like your dog — push me away, kick me, neglect me, abandon me. Just give me permission, unworthy as I am, to follow you. What lower place could I ask for in your love — and yet how highly I'd value it — than to be used the way you'd use your dog?
DEMETRIUS. Don't push my hatred too far. The sight of you makes me sick.
HELENA. And not seeing you makes me sick.

DEMETRIUS. You're putting your reputation at serious risk by leaving the city and putting yourself in the hands of someone who doesn't love you — trusting yourself to the dangers of a dark night and the bad influences of a deserted place, with the value of your virtue at stake.

HELENA. Your goodness is my protection. It isn't night when I can see your face, so I don't feel like I'm in the dark. And this forest isn't lacking for company, because to me, you are the whole world. So how can anyone say I'm alone when the whole world is right here looking at me?
DEMETRIUS. I'll run away from you and hide in the bushes, and leave you to the mercy of wild animals.

HELENA. The wildest animal doesn't have a heart as cruel as yours. Run as much as you like — the story's been reversed. Apollo flees, and Daphne gives chase. The dove chases the griffin. The gentle deer races to catch the tiger. Running is pointless when the coward flees and the brave one runs away!
DEMETRIUS. I'm done talking. Let me go. Or if you follow me, believe me, I'll do something you won't like in this forest.

HELENA. Yes, and in the temple, in the town, and in the open field, you already do me harm. Shame on you, Demetrius! Your cruelty is a disgrace to my entire sex. We women can't fight for love the way men can. We were meant to be courted, not to do the courting.
[Exit Demetrius.]
HELENA. I'll follow you and turn this hell into a heaven, even if it kills me — dying at the hand of the man I love so much.
[Exit Helena.]
OBERON. Good luck, girl. Before he leaves this forest, you'll be running from him, and he'll be chasing after your love.
[Enter Puck.]
OBERON. Have you got the flower? Welcome back, wanderer.
PUCK. Yes, here it is.

OBERON. Give it to me, please. I know a bank where wild thyme grows, where oxlips and nodding violets bloom, covered over with sweet honeysuckle, fragrant musk-roses, and wild rose. Titania sleeps there sometimes during the night, lulled among those flowers by dances and delight. Snakes shed their shiny skins there — skins wide enough to wrap a fairy in. I'll streak her eyes with this juice and fill her with horrible fantasies. Now take some of it and search through this forest. A sweet Athenian lady is in love with a young man who wants nothing to do with her. Put the juice on his eyes, but make sure the next thing he sees is the lady. You'll know the man by the Athenian clothes he's wearing. Do it carefully, so that he ends up more in love with her than she is with him. And make sure you meet me before the rooster crows at dawn.
PUCK. Don't worry, my lord. Your servant will get it done.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act II, Scene 2 — Another Part of the Wood
paragraphs: [Enter Titania with her Train.]

TITANIA. Come, let's have a dance and a fairy song. Then for just a moment, go off to your tasks. Some of you, kill the worms in the musk-rose buds. Some of you, fight the bats and take their leathery wings to make little coats for my fairies. And some of you, keep away the noisy owl that hoots every night, confused by our strange fairy ways. Now sing me to sleep. Then go about your work and let me rest.
[Fairies sing.]
FIRST FAIRY. You spotted snakes with your forked tongues, and thorny hedgehogs — stay away! Newts and slow-worms, do no wrong. Don't come near our Fairy Queen!

CHORUS. Nightingale, with your sweet melody, sing in our lovely lullaby. Hush, hush, lullaby; hush, hush, lullaby. Let no harm, no spell, no curse come near our beautiful lady. So good night, with a lullaby.
FIRST FAIRY. Weaving spiders, stay away from here! Get out, you long-legged spinners, get out! Black beetles, don't come near! Worms and snails, don't cause any harm!
CHORUS. Nightingale, with your sweet melody, and so on.
SECOND FAIRY. Go away now! All is well. One of you, stand guard at a distance.
[Exeunt Fairies. Titania sleeps.]
[Enter Oberon.]
OBERON. Whatever you see when you wake up —
[Squeezes the flower on  Titania's eyelids.]

OBERON. Fall in love with it as your one true love. Love and pine for its sake. Whether it's a wildcat, a bear, a leopard, or a wild boar with bristly hair — whatever appears before your eyes when you wake up, that will be your darling. Wake up when something horrible is near.
[Exit.]
[Enter Lysander and Hermia.]
LYSANDER. My love, you're exhausted from wandering through these woods. And to be honest, I've lost our way. Let's rest here, Hermia, if you agree, and wait for daylight.
HERMIA. All right, Lysander. You find yourself a place to sleep — I'll rest my head on this grassy bank.
LYSANDER. One patch of ground can be a pillow for both of us. One heart, one bed, two souls intertwined, one promise.
HERMIA. No, dear Lysander. For my sake, lie further away — don't lie so close to me.

LYSANDER. Oh, don't misunderstand my innocent intentions! When you're in love, you understand what love means. I mean that my heart is bound to yours so tightly that we share a single heart. Two souls linked by a vow — that makes two bodies but one promise. So don't refuse me a place beside you, because by lying next to you, Hermia, I'm not lying to you.

HERMIA. Lysander, you have a way with words. Now, shame on my manners and my pride if I thought you meant anything improper! But please, dear friend, for the sake of love and good manners, lie a bit further off — with enough distance between us to be appropriate for a respectable young man and woman. Stay that far apart, and good night, sweet friend. May your love never change until your life ends!
LYSANDER. Amen, amen to that beautiful prayer! And may my life end when my loyalty does! Here's my bed. I hope you sleep well!
HERMIA. I hope you get half as much rest as I wish for myself!
[They sleep.]
[Enter Puck.]

PUCK. I've gone through the whole forest but I haven't found any Athenian to test this flower's love-making power on. Night and silence! Who's this? He's wearing Athenian clothes — this must be the one my master said was treating the Athenian girl so badly. And there's the girl, sleeping on the damp, dirty ground. Poor thing, she didn't dare lie close to this loveless, rude man. You heartless fool — I'll throw all the power of this spell onto your eyes. When you wake up, may love keep sleep far from your eyelids. So wake up when I'm gone, because I need to get back to Oberon.
[Exit.]
[Enter Demetrius and Helena, running.]
HELENA. Stop! Even if you're going to kill me, stop, sweet Demetrius!
DEMETRIUS. Go away! I'm ordering you — stop following me like this!
HELENA. Are you really going to leave me here in the dark? Please don't.
DEMETRIUS. Stay here at your own risk. I'm going on alone.
[Exit Demetrius.]

HELENA. Oh, I'm completely out of breath from this ridiculous chase! The more I pray, the less I'm blessed. Hermia is lucky, wherever she's sleeping, because she has beautiful, appealing eyes. How did her eyes get so bright? Not from crying — if that's what it took, my eyes are washed with tears far more often than hers. No, I'm as ugly as a bear — wild animals run away from me in fear. So no wonder Demetrius flees from me as if I were a monster. What cruel, deceitful mirror made me think I could compare with Hermia's starry eyes? But who's this? Lysander, on the ground! Is he dead or asleep? I don't see any blood or wound. Lysander, if you're alive, please wake up.

LYSANDER. [Waking.] I'd run through fire for your sake! Radiant Helena! It's as if nature created a work of art, letting me see right through to your heart. Where is Demetrius? Oh, that vile name deserves to die on my sword!
HELENA. Don't say that, Lysander. What does it matter that he loves your Hermia? She still loves you. So be happy with that.

LYSANDER. Happy with Hermia? No — I regret every boring minute I spent with her. It's not Hermia I love, but Helena! Who wouldn't trade a raven for a dove? A man's desires are guided by his reason, and reason tells me you're the worthier woman. Things that grow aren't ripe until the right season. So I, being young, wasn't ripe for reason until now. Now that I've reached the peak of human understanding, reason has taken command of my heart and led me to your eyes, where I can read love stories written in love's most beautiful book.

HELENA. Why was I born to be mocked like this? When have I ever deserved this kind of scorn from you? Isn't it enough that I can never get a kind look from Demetrius — must you insult me too? Honestly, you're treating me terribly by pretending to court me this way. I thought you were a better man than this. Oh, to be rejected by one man and then made fun of by another!
[Exit.]

LYSANDER. She doesn't see Hermia lying there. Hermia, stay there and sleep — and may you never come near Lysander again! Just as too much of the sweetest food makes you sick to your stomach, or as people most hate the false beliefs they used to follow, you — my excess, my former delusion — I now hate you most of all! I'll devote all my energy and passion to honoring Helena and being her champion!
[Exit.]

HERMIA. [Starting.] Help me, Lysander, help me! Try your best to pull this crawling snake off my chest! Oh, have mercy! What a horrible dream that was! Lysander, look how I'm shaking with fear. I dreamed a snake was eating my heart, and you sat there smiling, watching it happen. Lysander! What — gone? Lysander, my lord! Are you out of earshot? Gone? Not a sound, not a word? Where are you? Speak if you can hear me! Speak, for the love of all that's dear! I'm almost fainting with fear. No answer? Then I see you're not here. I'll find either death or you right away.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 1 — The Wood
paragraphs: [The Queen of Fairies still lying asleep.]
[Enter Bottom, Quince, Snout, Starveling, Snug and Flute.]
BOTTOM. Is everyone here?

QUINCE. Right on time — and here's a wonderfully convenient place for our rehearsal. This green clearing will be our stage, this hawthorn thicket our backstage area. And we'll perform it with full action, just as we'll do it for the Duke.
BOTTOM. Peter Quince?
QUINCE. What is it, my good Bottom?

BOTTOM. There are some things in this comedy of Pyramus and Thisbe that will never go over well. First, Pyramus has to draw a sword and kill himself — and the ladies won't be able to handle that. What do you say to that?
SNOUT. Good heavens, that's a serious concern.
STARVELING. I think we'd better leave the killing out entirely.

BOTTOM. Not at all! I have a plan to make everything fine. Write me a prologue, and have the prologue explain that we won't do any real harm with our swords, and that Pyramus isn't really killed. And for even better reassurance, tell them that I, Pyramus, am not actually Pyramus but Bottom the weaver. That'll put them at ease.
QUINCE. All right, we'll have a prologue like that, and it'll be written in alternating lines of eight and six syllables.
BOTTOM. No, make it more — write it in eight and eight.
SNOUT. Won't the ladies be scared of the lion?
STARVELING. I'm afraid they will, I truly am.

BOTTOM. Gentlemen, you need to think about this carefully. To bring in — God protect us! — a lion among ladies is a most terrifying thing. There's no more frightening creature than a lion, and we need to be careful about it.
SNOUT. So we need another prologue to explain that he's not a real lion.

BOTTOM. No — you have to announce his name, and half his face has to be visible through the lion costume. And he himself has to speak through it, saying something like this — or words to that effect: "Ladies," or "Dear ladies, I would like you to know," or "I would ask you," or "I would beg you, not to be afraid, not to tremble: I swear on my life. If you think I'm a real lion, I feel sorry for my own life. No, I'm no such thing. I'm a man like any other man." And right there, he should give his name and tell them straight out that he's Snug the joiner.
QUINCE. All right, that's settled. But there are two more difficult problems. First, we need to bring moonlight into the room, because Pyramus and Thisbe meet by moonlight.
SNOUT. Does the moon shine on the night we perform our play?
BOTTOM. A calendar, a calendar! Check the almanac — find out about the moonlight!
QUINCE. Yes, the moon does shine that night.
BOTTOM. Well then, just leave one of the windows in the great hall open, and the moon can shine in through the window.

QUINCE. Right — or else someone has to come in carrying a bundle of thorns and a lantern, and say he's there to represent the moon. Then there's another issue: we need a wall in the great hall, because the story says Pyramus and Thisbe talked through a crack in a wall.
SNOUT. You can't exactly bring in a wall. What do you think, Bottom?

BOTTOM. Someone will have to play the Wall. He can cover himself with some plaster or some mud or some rough coating to look like a wall. And he holds his fingers apart like this, and Pyramus and Thisbe whisper through the gap.

QUINCE. If that works, then we're all set. Everyone sit down and rehearse your parts. Pyramus, you start. When you've finished your speech, exit into that thicket. And everyone else, enter on your cue.
[Enter Puck behind.]

PUCK. What rough country bumpkins do we have here, swaggering around so close to the Fairy Queen's resting place? What — a play in progress? I'll be in the audience. And maybe an actor too, if I see an opportunity.
QUINCE. Speak, Pyramus. Thisbe, step forward.
PYRAMUS. _Thisbe, the flowers have a sweet and foul smell —_
QUINCE. "Odors," not "odious."
PYRAMUS. _— odors, sweet smell. Your breath smells just as sweet, my dearest Thisbe dear. But wait, I hear a voice! Stay here for a moment, and I'll be right back._
[Exit.]
PUCK. A stranger Pyramus than has ever been seen here!
[Exit.]
THISBE. Do I speak now?
QUINCE. Yes, of course you do. He's only gone to check on a noise he heard, and he's supposed to come back.

THISBE. _Most radiant Pyramus, with skin as white as a lily, with a complexion as red as a rose on a triumphant bush, most lively young man, and also most lovely soul, as faithful as the most loyal horse that never tired — I'll meet you, Pyramus, at Ninny's tomb._

QUINCE. "Ninus's tomb," man! And why are you speaking that line yet? That's your answer to Pyramus. You've said your entire part all at once, cues and everything. Pyramus, enter! Your cue was "never tired."
THISBE. Oh — _As faithful as the most loyal horse that never tired._
[Enter Puck and Bottom with an ass's head.]
PYRAMUS. _If I were handsome, Thisbe, I'd be yours alone._
QUINCE. Oh, how horrible! Oh, how strange! We're haunted! Run, everyone, run! Help!
[Exeunt Clowns.]

PUCK. I'll chase after you! I'll lead you on a wild chase through bogs, through bushes, through thorns, through brambles. Sometimes I'll be a horse, sometimes a dog, a pig, a headless bear, sometimes a ball of fire. I'll neigh and bark and grunt and roar and blaze — taking the shape of horse, dog, pig, bear, fire at every turn!
[Exit.]
BOTTOM. Why are they running away? This is some trick of theirs to scare me.
[Enter Snout.]
SNOUT. Oh Bottom, you've been changed! What's that on your head?
BOTTOM. What do you see? You see a donkey's head of your own — is that it?
[Exit Snout.]
[Enter Quince.]
QUINCE. Bless you, Bottom, bless you! You've been transformed!
[Exit.]

BOTTOM. I see what they're up to. They're trying to make a fool of me, to scare me if they can. But I'm not moving from this spot, no matter what they do. I'll walk up and down here and sing, so they can hear that I'm not afraid.
[Sings.]
BOTTOM. The blackbird, so black of color, with his orange-brown beak, the thrush with his true, clear song, the wren with his tiny voice.
TITANIA. [Waking.] What angel wakes me from my bed of flowers?
[Sings.]

BOTTOM. The finch, the sparrow, and the lark, the plain-voiced cuckoo, gray, whose call many a man takes notice of, and no one dares to answer back — because really, who would try to argue with such a foolish bird? Who would call a bird a liar, even if it calls "cuckoo" over and over?

TITANIA. Please, gentle mortal, sing again. My ear is completely captivated by your voice. And my eye is enthralled by your form. The power of your fine qualities compels me, at first sight, to say — no, to swear — I love you.

BOTTOM. I'd say, ma'am, you don't have much reason for that. And yet, to be honest, reason and love don't keep much company these days. It's a shame that some decent neighbors won't help make them friends. Well, I can crack a joke when the occasion calls for it.
TITANIA. You are as wise as you are beautiful.
BOTTOM. Not really. But if I were smart enough to find my way out of this forest, that would be smart enough for my purposes.

TITANIA. Don't wish to leave this forest. You'll stay here whether you want to or not. I am no ordinary spirit. Summer itself attends upon me. And I love you — so come with me. I'll give you fairies to wait on you. They'll bring you jewels from the depths of the sea and sing to you while you sleep on a bed of pressed flowers. And I'll purify you of your mortal heaviness so that you'll move as lightly as a spirit. Peaseblossom! Cobweb! Moth! Mustardseed!
[Enter four Fairies.]
PEASEBLOSSOM. Ready.
COBWEB. And I.
MOTH. And I.
MUSTARDSEED. And I.
ALL. Where shall we go?

TITANIA. Be kind and attentive to this gentleman. Dance in his path and play before his eyes. Feed him with apricots and dewberries, with purple grapes, green figs, and mulberries. Steal the honey from the bumblebees, and for nighttime candles, take their waxy legs and light them from the glow-worm's eyes, so that my love has light when he goes to bed and when he wakes. Pluck the wings from painted butterflies to fan the moonbeams away from his sleeping eyes. Bow to him, elves, and show him your respect.
PEASEBLOSSOM. Greetings, mortal!
COBWEB. Greetings!
MOTH. Greetings!
MUSTARDSEED. Greetings!
BOTTOM. I beg your pardon, your worships. What is your name, if I may ask?
COBWEB. Cobweb.
BOTTOM. I'd like to get to know you better, Master Cobweb. If I cut my finger, I'll be sure to call on you for a bandage. And your name, good sir?
PEASEBLOSSOM. Peaseblossom.
BOTTOM. Please give my regards to Mrs. Squash, your mother, and to Mr. Peapod, your father. Master Peaseblossom, I'd like to get to know you better too. And your name, sir, if you please?
MUSTARDSEED. Mustardseed.

BOTTOM. Good Master Mustardseed, I know your patience well. That cowardly, giant-like roast beef has devoured many a member of your family. I promise you, your relatives have brought tears to my eyes before now. I'd like to get to know you better, good Master Mustardseed.

TITANIA. Come, attend to him. Lead him to my private retreat. The moon looks as though she's crying, I think, and whenever she weeps, every little flower weeps too, grieving over some violation of innocence. Gently quiet my love's tongue, and bring him along in silence.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act III, Scene 2 — Another Part of the Wood
paragraphs: [Enter Oberon.]
OBERON. I wonder if Titania has woken up yet — and what she saw first, which she's now helplessly in love with.
[Enter Puck.]
OBERON. Here comes my messenger. Well, mad spirit? What's been happening in this enchanted forest tonight?

PUCK. My mistress is in love with a monster. While she was sleeping near her private, sacred bower, a bunch of clumsy, rough working men who earn their living in the shops of Athens had gathered to rehearse a play they planned to perform at Theseus's wedding. The dullest, thickest-skinned fool of the whole sorry group — the one playing Pyramus — left the rehearsal area and wandered into a thicket. I took my chance and stuck a donkey's head on him. Right then, the actor playing Thisbe had to respond to his lines, and out comes my transformed fool. When his friends saw him, they scattered like wild geese spotting a hunter, or like a flock of jackdaws rising up and scattering at the sound of a gunshot. They flew in every direction, and as I stomped my foot, one of them kept tripping and falling. He screamed "Murder!" and called for help from Athens. They were so confused with fear that harmless things started attacking them — brambles and thorns snatched at their clothes, pulling off sleeves and hats. I chased them on in their panic and left sweet Pyramus standing there, transformed. And at that very moment, Titania woke up — and immediately fell in love with a donkey.
OBERON. This is turning out even better than I planned. But did you put the love juice on the Athenian's eyes like I told you to?
PUCK. I found him sleeping — that's done too. And the Athenian woman was right beside him, so she'd be the first thing he'd see when he woke up.
[Enter Demetrius and Hermia.]
OBERON. Step back and hide. This is the same Athenian.
PUCK. This is the woman — but that's not the man.
DEMETRIUS. Why are you being so harsh to someone who loves you so much? Save your bitter words for your bitter enemy.

HERMIA. I'm only scolding you now, but I should be treating you worse! Because I'm afraid you've killed Lysander in his sleep. You're already knee-deep in blood — you might as well dive in the rest of the way and kill me too! The sun was never more faithful to the day than Lysander was to me. Would he really have snuck away from sleeping Hermia? I'd sooner believe you could bore a hole through the entire earth and the moon could creep through the center to block the sun on the other side. It's impossible — you must have murdered him. A murderer should look like you do — so deathly pale and grim.

DEMETRIUS. That's how the murdered person should look — and that's how I look, pierced through the heart by your cruel words. Yet you, the one who murdered me, look as bright and clear as Venus shining in the evening sky.
HERMIA. What does that have to do with my Lysander? Where is he? Oh, Demetrius, please give him back to me.
DEMETRIUS. I'd rather give his body to my dogs.

HERMIA. Get away, you dog! You monster! You're pushing me past the limits of what a woman can endure! Have you really killed him? Then never call yourself a man again! Oh, just tell me the truth — tell me the truth, even if only for my sake! Would you have dared to look at him while he was awake? And did you kill him in his sleep? Oh, what a brave deed! A snake could have done as much. In fact, a snake did do it — because no snake ever stung with a more forked tongue than yours, you serpent.
DEMETRIUS. You're wasting your anger on a misunderstanding. I'm not guilty of Lysander's blood. As far as I know, he's not dead.
HERMIA. Then please tell me he's all right.
DEMETRIUS. And if I could, what would I get in return?
HERMIA. The privilege of never seeing me again. And with that, I'll leave your hateful presence. Whether he's dead or alive, just let me go.
[Exit.]

DEMETRIUS. There's no point chasing her when she's this furious. So I'll stay here for a while. Grief feels even heavier when you owe a debt of sleep — and now I'll pay a small part of that debt by resting here for a bit.
[Lies down.]
OBERON. What have you done? You made a mistake and put the love juice on the wrong man's eyes! Your error has inevitably turned a true love false, instead of turning a false love true.
PUCK. Well, that's fate for you. For every one man who keeps his promises, a million break theirs, piling oath upon oath.

OBERON. Go through the forest faster than the wind and find Helena of Athens. She's lovesick, pale-faced, and sighing — those sighs of love that drain the color from your cheeks. Use some trick to bring her here. I'll charm this man's eyes before she arrives.
PUCK. I'm going, I'm going! Watch how fast I go — swifter than an arrow from a warrior's bow!
[Exit.]

OBERON. Flower of this purple dye, struck by Cupid's arrow, sink into the center of his eye. When he sees the one who loves him, let her shine as gloriously as the goddess Venus in the sky. When you wake, if she's nearby, beg her for her love.
[Enter Puck.]
PUCK. Captain of our fairy band, Helena is close at hand. And the young man I mixed up is begging for a lover's reward. Shall we watch their ridiculous show? Lord, what fools these mortals are!
OBERON. Step aside. The noise they're making will wake Demetrius up.
PUCK. Then both men will be wooing the same woman at once. That should be entertaining all by itself. The things that please me most are the ones that go completely haywire.
[Enter Lysander and Helena.]

LYSANDER. Why would you think I'm mocking you? Mockery and scorn never come with tears. Look — when I make my vow, I weep. And promises born in tears carry the stamp of truth. How can these things seem like scorn to you when they carry the badge of sincerity to prove them real?

HELENA. You just keep getting cleverer and cleverer with your tricks. When one set of true vows contradicts another — what a devilish holy mess! These promises belong to Hermia. Will you just throw her away? If you weigh your vows to her against your vows to me, they'll balance perfectly — and both will be as empty as fairy tales.
LYSANDER. I had no good judgment when I made those promises to her.
HELENA. And you don't seem to have any now that you're breaking them.
LYSANDER. Demetrius loves her, and he doesn't love you.

DEMETRIUS. [Waking.] Oh Helena! Goddess, nymph, perfect, divine! What can I compare your eyes to, my love? Crystal looks murky next to them. Oh, how ripe and tempting your lips look, like kissing cherries! That pure white of your hand — the snow on the highest mountaintops turns dark by comparison when you hold up your hand. Oh, let me kiss this symbol of pure white beauty, this seal of happiness!

HELENA. Oh, how spiteful! Oh, this is awful! I can see you're all determined to gang up on me for your entertainment. If you had any manners or courtesy, you wouldn't treat me this badly. Can't you just hate me — which I know you do — without joining forces to mock me as well? If you were real men, as you appear to be, you wouldn't treat a gentle lady this way — making extravagant vows and over-praising my looks when I know you hate me in your hearts. You're both rivals who love Hermia, and now you've become rivals in mocking Helena. What a fine, manly thing to do — making a poor girl cry with your mockery! No one with any decency would torment a young woman this way, draining her patience just for sport.

LYSANDER. You're being unfair, Demetrius. Stop it. You love Hermia — you know that, and I know it. And here, with all my heart and goodwill, I give up my claim to Hermia's love. In return, give me your claim to Helena, whom I love and will love until I die.
HELENA. Nobody has ever wasted more breath on a joke.

DEMETRIUS. Lysander, keep your Hermia. I don't want her. If I ever loved her, that love is completely gone. My heart only visited with her temporarily — like a guest. But now it has come home to Helena, where it will stay.
LYSANDER. Helena, that's not true —
DEMETRIUS. Don't insult a loyalty you don't understand, or you'll pay dearly for it. Look — here comes your sweetheart now.
[Enter Hermia.]

HERMIA. The dark night takes away the power of sight, but it sharpens hearing instead. What the darkness takes from the eyes, it gives back double to the ears. I didn't find you with my eyes, Lysander — my ears led me to the sound of your voice. But why did you leave me so cruelly?
LYSANDER. Why would I stay when love was urging me to go?
HERMIA. What love could make Lysander leave my side?

LYSANDER. The love of Lysander — the love that wouldn't let him stay. Beautiful Helena, who lights up the night more brightly than all those fiery stars in the sky. Why are you looking for me? Didn't my leaving make it obvious that I hate you?
HERMIA. You can't mean what you're saying. That's impossible.

HELENA. So she's in on it too! Now I see — all three of them have conspired to create this cruel joke at my expense. Hermia, you ungrateful girl! Have you plotted with these men to torment me with this awful mockery? Have you forgotten all the secrets we shared, the sisterly vows, the hours we spent together, scolding time for moving too fast when we had to part? Have you forgotten all that? Our childhood friendship, our girlhood innocence? We were like two goddesses with our needlework, Hermia — creating the same flower with our needles, sitting on the same cushion, singing the same song in the same key, as if our hands, our sides, our voices, and our minds were all one. We grew together like a double cherry — appearing separate but actually joined, two lovely berries shaped on one stem. Two bodies, but one heart. Like two coats of arms joined under one crest. And you want to tear apart our old friendship to join with men in scorning your poor friend? This isn't friendly. This isn't how a woman should act. Every woman should be angry with you for this, though I'm the only one who feels the sting.
HERMIA. I'm completely bewildered by these passionate words. I'm not mocking you — it seems like you're mocking me.

HELENA. Didn't you put Lysander up to following me and praising my eyes and face, just to mock me? And didn't you get your other admirer, Demetrius — who just moments ago was pushing me away with his foot — to call me goddess, nymph, divine and rare, precious and celestial? Why would he say these things to a woman he hates? And why would Lysander deny his love for you — a love so deep in his soul — and offer me his affections, if not because you set them up to it, because you gave them permission? I may not be as popular as you, not as pursued by admirers, not as lucky — just miserably in love without being loved back. You should pity me rather than look down on me.
HERMIA. I have no idea what you're talking about.

HELENA. Sure, go ahead. Keep up the sad faces. Make faces at me when I turn my back. Wink at each other. Keep up this wonderful joke. This prank, if pulled off well, will go down in history. If you have any pity, grace, or good manners, you wouldn't make me the butt of your joke. But fine. It's partly my own fault — and death, or distance, will soon fix the problem.
LYSANDER. Stay, sweet Helena! Hear me out! My love, my life, my soul — beautiful Helena!
HELENA. Oh, wonderful!
HERMIA. Sweetheart, don't be so mean to her.
DEMETRIUS. If she can't persuade you to stop, I'll force you.

LYSANDER. You can't force me any more than she can persuade me. Your threats are no stronger than her gentle requests. Helena, I love you — on my life, I do! I swear by my very life, which I'd give up to prove that anyone who says I don't love you is a liar.
DEMETRIUS. I say I love you more than he ever could.
LYSANDER. If you really mean that, then step outside and prove it.
DEMETRIUS. Come on, then. Let's go.
HERMIA. Lysander, what is all this about?
LYSANDER. Get off me, you dark-skinned girl!
DEMETRIUS. No, no — he's just pretending to break free. He's acting like he wants to fight, but he won't actually come. You're all talk, man. Go on!
LYSANDER. Get off me, you cat, you burr! Let go of me, you disgusting creature, or I'll shake you off like a snake!
HERMIA. Why are you being so rude? What's changed? My sweet love —
LYSANDER. Your love? Get away from me, you dark-faced foreigner! Get away, you hated medicine! You loathsome potion — get out of my sight!
HERMIA. Are you joking?
HELENA. Yes, obviously — and so are you.
LYSANDER. Demetrius, I'll keep my promise to fight you.
DEMETRIUS. I wish I had a guarantee of that, because I can see you're held back by a pretty weak chain. I won't take your word for it.
LYSANDER. What — should I hit her, strike her, kill her? Even though I hate her, I won't hurt her like that.

HERMIA. What could you do that's worse than hating me? Hate me? Why? Oh, what's happened, my love? Am I not Hermia? Are you not Lysander? I'm just as beautiful now as I was before. You loved me when we fell asleep tonight, but when you woke up, you left me. Why? Oh, gods forbid! Do you really mean it?
LYSANDER. Yes, on my life. And I never want to see you again. So give up hope, give up questions, give up doubt. Be absolutely certain — it's no joke. I hate you, and I love Helena.
HERMIA. Oh no! You trickster! You poisonous flower! You thief of love! Did you sneak over in the night and steal my lover's heart?
HELENA. Oh, that's rich! Have you no shame, no modesty at all? Will you tear angry answers from my gentle tongue? Shame on you, you fraud! You puppet!

HERMIA. "Puppet"? Oh, so that's the game. Now I understand — she's been comparing our heights. She's been flaunting how tall she is, and she's used her height to win him over. So have you risen so high in his opinion because I'm so short? How short am I, you painted flagpole? Tell me — how short am I? I'm not so short that my fingernails can't reach your eyes!

HELENA. Please, gentlemen, even though you're mocking me, don't let her hurt me. I was never aggressive. I have no talent for fighting. I'm a proper coward. Don't let her hit me. You might think that because she's somewhat shorter than me, I could hold my own against her.
HERMIA. "Shorter"! There she goes again!

HELENA. Dear Hermia, please don't be so angry with me. I have always loved you, Hermia. I always kept your secrets and never wronged you — except that, because I love Demetrius, I told him about your plan to run away to this forest. He followed you, and I followed him out of love. But he drove me away and threatened to hit me, kick me, even kill me. And now, if you'll just let me leave in peace, I'll take my foolish heart back to Athens and stop following you. Let me go. You can see how simple and foolish I am.
HERMIA. Fine, go then. Who's stopping you?
HELENA. A foolish heart that I'm leaving behind here.
HERMIA. What — with Lysander?
HELENA. With Demetrius.
LYSANDER. Don't worry, Helena. She won't hurt you.
DEMETRIUS. She certainly won't — not even with you defending her.
HELENA. Oh, when she's angry, she's sharp and vicious. She was a little terror when we were in school together. And even though she's small, she's fierce.
HERMIA. "Little" again! Nothing but "short" and "little"? Why do you let her insult me like this? Let me get at her!
LYSANDER. Get out of here, you dwarf! You tiny thing, made from knotgrass! You bead! You acorn!

DEMETRIUS. You're being too helpful on behalf of someone who despises your help. Leave her alone. Don't speak about Helena. Don't take her side — because if you show even the smallest hint of love for her, you'll pay for it.
LYSANDER. Now Hermia's not holding me back anymore. Follow me if you dare, and let's settle whose claim to Helena is greater — yours or mine.
DEMETRIUS. Follow you? No — I'll walk right beside you, face to face.
[Exeunt Lysander and Demetrius.]
HERMIA. You! This whole mess is your fault. No — don't back away.
HELENA. I don't trust you, and I'm not staying in your company any longer. Your fists are quicker than mine in a fight. But my legs are longer — for running away.
[Exit.]
HERMIA. I'm stunned. I don't know what to say.
[Exit, pursuing Helena.]
OBERON. This is your fault. You always make mistakes — or else you do these things on purpose.

PUCK. Believe me, king of shadows, it was an honest mistake. Didn't you tell me I'd recognize the man by the Athenian clothes he was wearing? Well, I did put the love juice on an Athenian's eyes — so I completed my mission correctly. And as far as I'm concerned, their argument is great entertainment.

OBERON. You see these lovers are looking for a place to fight. So hurry, Robin — cover the night sky with thick fog, as black as the underworld, and lead these hotheaded rivals so far astray that they can never find each other. Sometimes imitate Lysander's voice, then provoke Demetrius with insults. Sometimes sound like Demetrius. Lead them apart from each other this way until a deathlike sleep creeps over them on heavy, tired legs. Then crush this herb into Lysander's eye — its juice has the power to remove all the enchantment and restore his sight to normal. When they all wake up, everything that happened will seem like a dream and a meaningless vision. The lovers will return to Athens, bound together in partnerships that will last until death. While you handle this, I'll go to my queen and ask for the Indian boy. Then I'll release her enchanted eyes from the spell, and everything will be at peace.

PUCK. My fairy lord, we need to hurry. Night's swift dragons are racing across the clouds, and the morning star is already shining over there. At its approach, wandering ghosts hurry home to the graveyards. The damned spirits who are buried at crossroads and in rivers have already gone back to their wormy beds, afraid of being caught by daylight. They choose to exile themselves from light and must forever keep company with dark night.

OBERON. But we are spirits of a different kind. I've often made sport with the dawn, and like a forester, I can walk through the groves until the fiery-red eastern sky opens up and turns the ocean's salt-green waters to gold with its blessed beams. But still, hurry — don't delay. We can finish this business before daybreak.
[Exit Oberon.]
PUCK. Up and down, up and down — I'll lead them up and down. I'm feared in the countryside and in the town. Come on, goblin, lead them up and down. Here comes one now.
[Enter Lysander.]
LYSANDER. Where are you, proud Demetrius? Speak up!
PUCK. Right here, villain — armed and ready! Where are you?
LYSANDER. I'm coming for you right now!
PUCK. Then follow me to more open ground.
[Exit Lysander as following the voice.]
[Enter Demetrius.]
DEMETRIUS. Lysander! Speak again! You runaway, you coward — have you fled? Speak up! Are you hiding in some bush?

PUCK. You coward! Are you bragging to the stars, telling the bushes you're looking for a fight, but you won't actually come? Come out, you weakling, you child! I'll whip you with a stick. Any man who draws a sword on you would disgrace himself.
DEMETRIUS. Are you there?
PUCK. Follow my voice. We'll settle this somewhere else.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Lysander.]

LYSANDER. He keeps running ahead of me and daring me to follow. But every time I get to where he's calling from, he's gone. The villain is much quicker on his feet than I am. I ran fast, but he ran faster, and now I've stumbled onto this dark, uneven path. I'll rest here. Come, gentle daylight!
[Lies down.] Because as soon as you show me your first gray light, I'll find Demetrius and get my revenge. [Sleeps.]
[Enter Puck and Demetrius.]
PUCK. Ha ha ha! Coward — why won't you come and fight?
DEMETRIUS. Wait for me if you dare! I know perfectly well you keep running ahead of me, changing your position, and you won't stand still or look me in the face. Where are you?
PUCK. Over here! Come here!

DEMETRIUS. No — you're just mocking me. You'll pay dearly for this if I ever see your face in daylight. Go your way for now. I'm too exhausted to keep chasing you, and I need to stretch out on this cold ground. Expect me to come looking for you at dawn.
[Lies down and sleeps.]
[Enter Helena.]

HELENA. Oh, weary night! Oh long and tedious night! Make your hours shorter! Shine, eastern dawn, so I can find my way back to Athens by daylight and get away from the people who despise my company. And sleep, which sometimes closes the eyes of sorrow — steal me away from my own miserable self for a while.
[Sleeps.]
PUCK. Only three so far? Come on, one more. Two of each kind makes four. Here she comes — upset and angry. Cupid is a wicked little troublemaker, driving these poor women crazy like this.
[Enter Hermia.]

HERMIA. I have never been so tired, never so miserable — soaked with dew and torn by brambles. I can't crawl another step, can't go any further. My legs can't keep up with my wishes. I'll rest here until daybreak. Heaven protect Lysander if those two are fighting!
[Lies down.]
PUCK. Lie on the ground and sleep soundly. I'll apply this remedy to your eye, gentle lover.
[Squeezing the juice on Lysander's eye.]

PUCK. When you wake, you'll take true delight in the sight of the woman you really love. And the old proverb that everyone knows — that every man should end up with the right one — will come true when you open your eyes. Jack shall have Jill, nothing shall go wrong. The man shall get his girl again, and all shall be well.
[Exit Puck.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 1 — The Wood
paragraphs: [Lysander, Demetrius, Helena and Hermia still asleep.]
[Enter Titania and Bottom; Peaseblossom, Cobweb, Moth, Mustardseed and other Fairies attending; Oberon behind, unseen.]
TITANIA. Come, sit down on this bed of flowers. Let me stroke your lovely cheeks and put musk-roses in your smooth, sleek hair, and kiss your fine, large ears, my gentle darling.
BOTTOM. Where's Peaseblossom?
PEASEBLOSSOM. Ready.
BOTTOM. Scratch my head, Peaseblossom. Where's Monsieur Cobweb?
COBWEB. Ready.

BOTTOM. Monsieur Cobweb — be a good fellow and grab your weapons and kill me a red-bottomed bumblebee on top of a thistle. And be a good chap and bring me the honey sac. But don't tire yourself out too much doing it, Monsieur. And be careful the honey sac doesn't burst — I wouldn't want you drowning in honey, sir. Where's Monsieur Mustardseed?
MUSTARDSEED. Ready.
BOTTOM. Give me your fist, Monsieur Mustardseed. No need for bowing and scraping, good Monsieur.
MUSTARDSEED. What would you like?

BOTTOM. Nothing, good Monsieur, just help Sir Cobweb with the scratching. I need to get to the barber's, Monsieur, because I think I've gotten remarkably hairy around the face. And I'm such a sensitive donkey that if even one hair tickles me, I have to scratch.
TITANIA. Would you like to hear some music, my sweet love?
BOTTOM. I have a pretty good ear for music. Let's have the tongs and the bones — some simple percussion.
TITANIA. Or tell me, sweet love, what you'd like to eat.
BOTTOM. Honestly, a good helping of animal feed. I could really go for some nice, dry oats. Actually, I think I'd love a bale of hay — good hay, sweet hay, there's nothing like it.
TITANIA. I have an adventurous fairy who'll search out a squirrel's stash and bring you fresh nuts.
BOTTOM. I'd rather have a handful or two of dried peas. But please, don't let any of your people disturb me — I feel a powerful urge to sleep coming over me.

TITANIA. Sleep, then, and I'll wrap my arms around you. Fairies, leave us — scatter in every direction. Just as the honeysuckle gently twists around the sweet vine, and the female ivy wraps itself around the rough bark of the elm tree — oh, how I love you! How I adore you!
[They sleep.]
[Oberon advances. Enter Puck.]

OBERON. Welcome, good Robin. Do you see this touching sight? I'm starting to pity her infatuation. When I ran into her recently in the woods, looking for lovely flowers to crown this disgusting fool, I scolded her and argued with her. She had encircled his hairy temples with a wreath of fresh, fragrant flowers. And the same dew that usually swells on flower buds like round, gleaming pearls was now standing in the little flowers' eyes like tears weeping over their own disgrace. After I had teased her to my heart's content, and she had meekly begged for my patience, I asked her for the changeling boy. She gave him to me at once, and sent her fairy to carry him to my home in fairyland. And now that I have the boy, I'll undo this hateful spell on her eyes. And, gentle Puck, remove this transformed donkey's head from the Athenian workman, so that when he wakes up with the others, they can all go back to Athens and think of this night's events as nothing more than the wild confusion of a dream. But first, I'll release the Fairy Queen from her spell.
[Touching her eyes with an herb.]
OBERON. Be as you used to be. See as you used to see. The power of Diana's flower has conquered Cupid's. Now, my Titania — wake up, my sweet queen.
TITANIA. My Oberon! What strange visions I've had! I dreamed I was in love with a donkey.
OBERON. There lies your sweetheart.
TITANIA. How did this happen? Oh, how my eyes hate the sight of him now!
OBERON. Quiet for a moment. Robin, take off that head. Titania, call for music — and let it put all five of these sleepers into a deeper trance than ordinary sleep.
TITANIA. Music! Play music — the kind that enchants people to sleep!
PUCK. Now when you wake up, you'll see with your own foolish eyes again.
OBERON. Play the music.
[Still music.]

OBERON. Come, my queen, take my hand, and let's gently rock the ground where these sleepers lie. Now you and I are friends again, and tomorrow at midnight we'll dance solemnly in Duke Theseus's house in celebration, and bless it with lasting good fortune. The faithful pairs of lovers will be married there, alongside Theseus, all in joy.
PUCK. Fairy king, listen — I can hear the morning lark singing.
OBERON. Then, my queen, let us follow the fading night in silence. We can circle the globe quickly — faster than the wandering moon.
TITANIA. Come, my lord. And as we fly, tell me how it happened that I was found sleeping here on the ground among these mortals.
[Exeunt. Horns sound within.]
[Enter Theseus, Hippolyta, Egeus and Train.]

THESEUS. Send someone to find the forester. Our early morning rituals are done, and since we have the early part of the day ahead of us, my love will enjoy the music of my hunting hounds. Release them in the western valley and let them run. Go on — find the forester.
[Exit an Attendant.]
THESEUS. We'll go up to the mountaintop, my beautiful queen, and listen to the wonderful music the hounds and the echoes make together.

HIPPOLYTA. I was once with Hercules and Cadmus when they hunted a bear with Spartan hounds in a forest in Crete. I never heard such magnificent barking — the groves, the skies, the fountains, every nearby place seemed to merge into one great chorus. I never heard such musical chaos, such sweet thunder.

THESEUS. My hounds are bred from the Spartan line — they have drooping jowls and sandy coats, their heads hang low with ears that sweep the morning dew. They're bow-legged and have loose skin at their throats like Thessalian bulls. Slow in the chase, but their barking harmonizes like a peal of bells, each deeper than the last. A more tuneful pack was never encouraged with horns — not in Crete, not in Sparta, not in Thessaly. Judge for yourself when you hear them. But wait — what young people are these?
EGEUS. My lord, this is my daughter, asleep here. And this is Lysander. This one is Demetrius. And this is Helena, old Nedar's daughter Helena. I'm amazed to find them here together.

THESEUS. No doubt they got up early to celebrate May Day. And hearing about our plans, they came here to honor our celebration. But tell me, Egeus — isn't this the day Hermia is supposed to give her answer about her choice?
EGEUS. It is, my lord.
THESEUS. Go tell the huntsmen to wake them with their horns.
[Horns, and shout within. Demetrius, Lysander, Hermia and Helena wake and start up.]
THESEUS. Good morning, friends! Valentine's Day is past. Are you wood-birds only just now pairing up?
LYSANDER. Forgive us, my lord.
[He and the rest kneel to  Theseus.]

THESEUS. Please, all of you, stand up. I know you two are rivals. How is it that such peaceful harmony has come about, when hatred is so far from jealousy that enemies can sleep side by side without fear?

LYSANDER. My lord, I'll answer as best I can, half asleep and half awake. I honestly can't say exactly how I got here. But as I think about it — and I want to speak truthfully — now I remember: I came here with Hermia. We planned to leave Athens, where we could escape the danger of Athenian law.

EGEUS. Enough! That's enough, my lord! You've heard enough! I demand the law be enforced against him! They were trying to run away — they were, Demetrius! — planning to cheat both of us. You of your wife, and me of my right to decide whom she should marry.

DEMETRIUS. My lord, Helena told me about their plan to escape to this forest. I followed them here in a fury, and Helena followed me out of love. But, my good lord — I don't know by what power, though some power has clearly been at work — my love for Hermia has melted away like snow. It now seems to me like the memory of some worthless toy I was obsessed with as a child. All the faith, all the devotion of my heart, the object of my eye's desire and pleasure — all of it belongs to Helena alone. I was engaged to her before I ever saw Hermia. I rejected that love like a sick person rejects food. But now, in full health, my natural appetite has returned. Now I want her, I love her, I long for her, and I will be true to her forever.

THESEUS. Well, lovers, this is a fortunate meeting. We'll hear more about all this later. Egeus, I'm going to overrule your wishes. These two couples will be married together in the temple, right alongside us. And since the morning is already getting late, we'll skip the hunt we had planned. Come along — let's all go back to Athens. Three couples and three — we'll celebrate with a great feast. Come, Hippolyta.
[Exeunt Theseus, Hippolyta, Egeus and Train.]
DEMETRIUS. Everything seems so small and blurry — like distant mountains that look like clouds.
HERMIA. I feel like I'm seeing everything double, with my eyes crossed.
HELENA. I feel the same way. And I've found Demetrius like a jewel — mine and yet somehow not really mine.
DEMETRIUS. Are you sure we're actually awake? It seems to me like we're still sleeping, still dreaming. Didn't the Duke just come here and tell us to follow him?
HERMIA. Yes — and my father was here too.
HELENA. And Hippolyta.
LYSANDER. And he told us to follow him to the temple.
DEMETRIUS. Then we really are awake. Let's follow him, and we can compare our dreams along the way.
[Exeunt.]

BOTTOM. [Waking.] When my cue comes, call me and I'll answer. My next line is "Most fair Pyramus." Hey! Peter Quince! Flute the bellows-mender! Snout the tinker! Starveling! Good God — they've all snuck off and left me here asleep! I've had the most extraordinary vision. I've had a dream that is beyond any man's ability to describe. Anyone who tries to explain this dream is a complete donkey. I thought I was — no man can say what. I thought I was, and I thought I had — but anyone who tries to say what I thought I had is a patched-together fool. No human eye has heard, no human ear has seen, no human hand can taste, no human tongue can imagine, and no human heart can express what my dream was. I'm going to get Peter Quince to write a ballad about this dream. It'll be called "Bottom's Dream," because it has no bottom — no explanation. And I'll sing it at the end of a play, before the Duke. And maybe, to make it even more moving, I'll sing it at the death scene.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act IV, Scene 2 — Athens. A Room in Quince's House
paragraphs: [Enter Quince, Flute, Snout and Starveling.]
QUINCE. Has anyone sent word to Bottom's house? Has he come home yet?
STARVELING. Nobody's heard from him. He must have been carried off somewhere.
FLUTE. If he doesn't come back, the play is ruined. We can't go on without him, can we?
QUINCE. Absolutely not. There isn't another man in all of Athens who can play Pyramus except him.
FLUTE. No, he truly has the finest mind of any working man in Athens.
QUINCE. Yes, and the best-looking too. And he's an absolute dream when it comes to a sweet voice.
FLUTE. You mean "paragon." A "paramour" is — God help us — something indecent.
[Enter Snug.]
SNUG. Friends, the Duke has just come from the temple, and two or three more lords and ladies have gotten married. If our show had gone ahead, we'd all have made our fortunes.

FLUTE. Oh, dear Bottom! He's lost himself a guaranteed pension for life. He couldn't have avoided getting paid at least sixpence a day. If the Duke hadn't given him sixpence a day for playing Pyramus, I'll eat my hat. He would have deserved it — sixpence a day for Pyramus, or nothing at all.
[Enter Bottom.]
BOTTOM. Where are my boys? Where are my brave lads?
QUINCE. Bottom! Oh, what a wonderful day! Oh, what a happy moment!
BOTTOM. Friends, I have amazing things to tell you — but don't ask me what, because if I tell you, I'm not a true Athenian. I'll tell you everything exactly as it happened.
QUINCE. Tell us, dear Bottom!

BOTTOM. Not a word about what happened to me. All I'll tell you is that the Duke has finished dining. Get your costumes together — good strings to attach your beards, new ribbons for your shoes. Meet at the palace right away. Everyone look over your part one last time. The long and short of it is, our play has been selected! And whatever you do, make sure Thisbe has clean clothes. And the man who plays the lion shouldn't trim his nails — they need to stick out as the lion's claws. And my dear actors, don't eat any onions or garlic, because we need to have sweet breath. And I have no doubt they'll say it's a sweet comedy. No more talking — let's go! Move!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act V, Scene 1 — Athens. An Apartment in the Palace of Theseus
paragraphs: [Enter Theseus, Hippolyta, Philostrate, Lords and Attendants.]
HIPPOLYTA. The things these lovers describe are very strange, my Theseus.

THESEUS. Stranger than they are true. I can't bring myself to believe these old fairy tales and fantasy stories. Lovers and madmen have such overheated brains, such powerful imaginations, that they perceive more than cool reason can ever understand. The madman, the lover, and the poet are all made entirely of imagination. One sees more devils than all of hell can hold — that's the madman. The lover, just as frantic, sees the beauty of Helen of Troy in an ordinary face. The poet's eye, rolling in a fine frenzy, glances from heaven to earth and from earth to heaven. And as the imagination gives shape to unknown things, the poet's pen turns them into forms and gives each airy nothing a specific place and a name. This is the power of strong imagination — if it wants to feel some joy, it invents a source for that joy. Or at night, when you're imagining something scary, how easy it is to mistake a bush for a bear!
