HIPPOLYTA. But the whole story of last night, told by all of them together, with all their minds transformed in the same way — it adds up to something more than just imagination. It takes on a strange but real consistency. Whatever happened, it's certainly strange and remarkable.
[Enter lovers: Lysander, Demetrius, Hermia and Helena.]
THESEUS. Here come the lovers, full of joy and happiness! Welcome, dear friends! May joy and fresh days of love accompany your hearts!
LYSANDER. May even more than that wait for you — in your royal halls, at your table, and in your bed!

THESEUS. Now then — what entertainments, what dances shall we have to fill these three long hours between our supper and bedtime? Where is our usual master of entertainment? What celebrations are planned? Is there no play to help pass this agonizingly long evening? Call Philostrate.
PHILOSTRATE. Here, mighty Theseus.
THESEUS. Tell me — what entertainment do you have for tonight? What masquerade? What music? How shall we fill this idle time if not with some amusement?
PHILOSTRATE. Here is a list of several entertainments that are ready to be performed. Choose which one your Highness would like to see first.
[Giving a paper.]

THESEUS. [Reads] "The Battle with the Centaurs, to be sung by an Athenian eunuch to the harp." No, we won't have that. I've already told my love about that in praise of my relative Hercules. "The Riot of the Drunken Revelers, tearing apart the Thracian singer in their madness." That's an old show — it was performed when I last returned as a conqueror from Thebes. "The Three Times Three Muses Mourning for the Death of Learning, Recently Deceased in Poverty." That's some kind of sharp social commentary — not appropriate for a wedding celebration. "A Tedious Brief Scene of Young Pyramus and His Love Thisbe: Very Tragical Mirth." Merry and tragic? Tedious and brief? That's like hot ice and wonderfully strange snow. How can we make sense of this contradiction?

PHILOSTRATE. It's a play, my lord, about ten words long — which makes it as brief as any play I've ever seen. But even at ten words, my lord, it's too long — which makes it tedious. Because in the entire play, not one word is well-chosen, and not one actor is right for his part. And it is tragic, my noble lord — because Pyramus kills himself in it. When I watched the rehearsal, I must admit it made my eyes water. But they were tears of laughter — the most hilarious tears that passionate, loud laughter has ever produced.
THESEUS. Who are the performers?
PHILOSTRATE. Working men from Athens who have never exercised their minds before. And now they've strained their unpracticed memories to learn this play for your wedding.
THESEUS. And we will watch it.

PHILOSTRATE. No, my noble lord — it's not suitable for you. I've watched it through, and it's absolutely nothing. Unless you can find entertainment in their sincere efforts — which have been agonizingly rehearsed with painful dedication — all to serve you.
THESEUS. I will watch that play. Nothing can go truly wrong when it's offered with simplicity and genuine devotion. Go bring them in, and take your seats, ladies.
[Exit Philostrate.]
HIPPOLYTA. I don't enjoy watching people overwhelmed by a task beyond their abilities, struggling and failing in their service.
THESEUS. Don't worry, my sweet — you won't see anything like that.
HIPPOLYTA. He says they can't do anything of this kind.

THESEUS. All the more reason for us to be kind and thank them for their effort. Our entertainment will come from appreciating what they get wrong. And when humble people can't manage their duty, noble minds accept the intention rather than judging the result. In my experience, great scholars have planned elaborate welcome speeches for me. I've watched them shiver and turn pale, lose their place mid-sentence, choke on their rehearsed words out of nervousness, and finally just go silent without completing their welcome. Trust me, sweetheart — from that silence, I still gathered a warm welcome. And in the modesty of fearful devotion, I read as much meaning as I do from the glib tongue of bold, confident eloquence. Love and tongue-tied simplicity speak the most to me, with the fewest words.
[Enter Philostrate.]
PHILOSTRATE. If it please your Grace, the speaker of the Prologue is ready.
THESEUS. Let him come forward.
[Flourish of trumpets. Enter the Prologue.]

PROLOGUE. If we offend, it is with our good will. That you should think we come not to offend, but with good will. To show our simple skill, that is the true beginning of our end. Consider then, we come but in spite. We do not come as wanting to please you. Our true intent is all for your delight. We are not here that you should here regret. The actors are at hand, and by their show you shall know all that you are likely to know.
THESEUS. This fellow doesn't pay any attention to punctuation.
LYSANDER. He rode through his prologue like a man on an unbroken horse — he doesn't know where to stop. A good lesson, my lord: it's not enough to speak — you have to speak clearly.
HIPPOLYTA. He played that prologue like a child playing a recorder — making sound, but with no control over it.
THESEUS. His speech was like a tangled chain — all the links were there, but completely jumbled. Who's next?
[Enter Pyramus and Thisbe, Wall, Moonshine and Lion as in dumb show.]

PROLOGUE. Ladies and gentlemen, you may wonder at this show. But keep wondering until the truth makes everything clear. This man is Pyramus, in case you were wondering. This beautiful lady is certainly Thisbe. This man, covered in plaster and rough coating, represents Wall — that terrible wall that kept these lovers apart. Through Wall's crack, the poor souls are happy to whisper — don't be surprised by that. This man with the lantern, dog, and thornbush represents Moonshine. Because, you should know, these lovers didn't think it beneath them to meet by moonlight at Ninus's tomb — there, right there, to woo each other. This frightening beast, whose name is Lion, scared the faithful Thisbe when she arrived first at night — or rather, frightened her. And as she ran away, she dropped her cloak. The vile Lion stained it with his bloody mouth. Soon after, sweet, tall young Pyramus arrives and finds his faithful Thisbe's cloak, all bloodied. At that, with his blade — his bloody, guilty blade — he bravely stabbed himself in the chest. And Thisbe, waiting in the shade of a mulberry tree, drew his dagger and died as well. As for the rest, let Lion, Moonshine, Wall, and the two lovers explain at length while they remain here.
[Exeunt Prologue, Pyramus, Thisbe, Lion and Moonshine.]
THESEUS. I wonder if the lion is going to speak.
DEMETRIUS. No surprise there, my lord. One lion might speak when so many donkeys do.

WALL. In this play, it so happens that I, a man named Snout, play a wall. And it's the kind of wall I'd like you to imagine has a cracked hole or chink in it, through which the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe often whispered very secretly. This plaster, this rough coating, and this stone are meant to show that I am indeed that wall. And this here is the crack — right here — through which the nervous lovers are supposed to whisper.
THESEUS. Could you ask for plaster and mortar to deliver a better speech?
DEMETRIUS. It's the wittiest wall I've ever heard speak, my lord.
THESEUS. Pyramus approaches the wall. Quiet, everyone.
[Enter Pyramus.]

PYRAMUS. Oh, grim-looking night! Oh, night so black! Oh, night, which always comes when day does not! Oh, night, oh night — alas, alas, alas! I'm afraid my Thisbe has forgotten her promise! And you, oh Wall — oh sweet, oh lovely Wall — you who stand between her father's property and mine! You Wall, oh Wall, oh sweet and lovely Wall — show me your crack so I can peek through with my eyes!
[Wall holds up his fingers.]

PYRAMUS. Thanks, kind Wall! May the gods protect you for this! But what do I see? I don't see any Thisbe! Oh, wicked Wall — through you I see no happiness! Curse your stones for deceiving me like this!
THESEUS. It seems to me that the Wall, since it has feelings, should curse back.

PYRAMUS. No, truly, sir, he shouldn't. "Deceiving me" is Thisbe's cue — she's supposed to enter now, and I'm supposed to spot her through the wall. You'll see — it'll happen exactly as I told you. Here she comes.
[Enter Thisbe.]
THISBE. Oh Wall, you have so often heard my sighs, keeping my beautiful Pyramus and me apart! My cherry lips have often kissed your stones — your stones held together with plaster and mortar.
PYRAMUS. I see a voice! Now I'll go to the crack and see if I can hear my Thisbe's face. Thisbe!
THISBE. It's my love, I think — my love!
PYRAMUS. Think what you will — I am your lover's grace. And like Leander, I am faithful still.
THISBE. And I am like Helen, until the day fate kills me.
PYRAMUS. Cephalus was never so true to Procris.
THISBE. As Cephalus to Procris, I am true to you.
PYRAMUS. Oh, kiss me through the hole in this terrible wall!
THISBE. I'm kissing the wall's hole, not your lips at all.
PYRAMUS. Will you meet me right away at Ninny's tomb?
THISBE. Come life, come death — I'll be there without delay!
WALL. And so I, Wall, have played my part. And now that it's done, Wall goes away.
[Exeunt Wall, Pyramus and Thisbe.]
THESEUS. And now the wall between the two neighbors has come down.
DEMETRIUS. Nothing to be done about it, my lord — not when walls are so eager to eavesdrop without warning.
HIPPOLYTA. This is the most ridiculous thing I've ever seen.
THESEUS. The best works of this kind are still only illusions. And the worst are no worse, if our imagination fills in the gaps.
HIPPOLYTA. It'll have to be your imagination then, not theirs.
THESEUS. If we think no worse of them than they think of themselves, they can pass for excellent performers. Here come two noble beasts — a man and a lion.
[Enter Lion and Moonshine.]

LION. You ladies, whose gentle hearts are afraid of the smallest little mouse that scurries across the floor — you may perhaps both tremble and shake when a rough lion roars in his wildest fury. So let me tell you: I am only Snug the joiner. I'm a fierce lion in costume, nothing more. Because if I were actually to charge into this place as a real lion, I'd be putting my life at risk.
THESEUS. A very gentle beast, and with a clear conscience.
DEMETRIUS. The finest beast-performer, my lord, that I've ever seen.
LYSANDER. This lion is about as brave as a fox.
THESEUS. True — and about as clever as a goose.
DEMETRIUS. Not quite, my lord — his bravery can't carry his brains, just as a fox carries a goose.
THESEUS. His brains certainly can't carry his bravery — a goose doesn't carry a fox. Fair enough. Leave it to his discretion, and let's listen to what the moon has to say.
MOONSHINE. This lantern represents the horned moon.
DEMETRIUS. He should have worn the horns on his head.
THESEUS. He's not a crescent moon, and his horns are invisible within the circle.
MOONSHINE. This lantern represents the horned moon. I myself am supposed to be the man in the moon.
THESEUS. That's the biggest mistake of all — the man should be inside the lantern. How else is he the man in the moon?
DEMETRIUS. He doesn't dare go in there because of the candle — you can see it's already burning low and getting cranky.
HIPPOLYTA. I'm tired of this moon. I wish it would change!
THESEUS. Judging by his dim performance, he does seem to be waning. But in courtesy and fairness, we should let him finish.
LYSANDER. Go ahead, Moon.
MOON. All I have to say is this: the lantern is the moon, I'm the man in the moon, this thornbush is my thornbush, and this dog is my dog.
DEMETRIUS. All of those things should be inside the lantern, since they're all in the moon. But quiet — here comes Thisbe.
[Enter Thisbe.]
THISBE. This is old Ninus's tomb. Where is my love?
LION. Rawr!
[The Lion roars, Thisbe runs off.]
DEMETRIUS. Well roared, Lion!
THESEUS. Well run, Thisbe!
HIPPOLYTA. Well done, Moon! Truly, the moon shines with great style.
[The Lion tears Thisbe's mantle, and exit.]
THESEUS. Well pounced, Lion!
DEMETRIUS. And then came Pyramus.
LYSANDER. And the lion disappeared.
[Enter Pyramus.]

PYRAMUS. Sweet Moon, I thank you for your sunny beams! I thank you, Moon, for shining now so bright! For by your gracious, golden, glittering gleams, I hope to catch a glimpse of my true Thisbe! But wait — oh no! But look, poor fellow, what a terrible sight is here! Eyes, do you see? How can this be? Oh, precious darling! Oh, dear! Your fine cloak — what? Stained with blood? Come, Furies of vengeance! Oh Fates, come, come! Cut the thread of life, cut it right through! Tremble, rush, destroy, and kill!
THESEUS. This display of grief, combined with the death of a close friend, might almost make a person look sad.
HIPPOLYTA. I swear, I actually feel sorry for the man.

PYRAMUS. Oh Nature, why did you ever create lions, since a vile lion has destroyed my darling? She was — no, no — she was the most beautiful woman who ever lived, who ever loved, who ever liked, who ever looked with cheer. Come, tears, overwhelm me! Come out, sword, and stab the chest of Pyramus! Yes, this left side of my chest, where the heart beats — and so I die, like this, like this, like this! Now I am dead. Now I am gone. My soul is in the sky. Tongue, lose your light! Moon, take your flight! Now die, die, die, die, die!
[Dies. Exit Moonshine.]
DEMETRIUS. Not a "die" as in a dice — just an "ace," because he's only one.
LYSANDER. Less than an ace, actually. He's dead — he's nothing.
THESEUS. With the help of a surgeon, he might still recover and turn out to be a donkey.
HIPPOLYTA. Why did Moonshine leave before Thisbe comes back to find her lover?
THESEUS. She'll find him by starlight.
[Enter Thisbe.]
THESEUS. Here she comes, and her grief will end the play.
HIPPOLYTA. I hope she'll keep it short for a Pyramus like this one.
DEMETRIUS. The tiniest speck would tip the scales between which one is better — Pyramus or Thisbe. He as a man, God help us. She as a woman, God bless us!
LYSANDER. She's already spotted him with those sweet eyes of hers.
DEMETRIUS. And now she begins her lament — that is to say —

THISBE. Asleep, my love? What — dead, my dove? Oh, Pyramus, get up! Speak, speak! Completely silent? Dead, dead? A grave must cover your sweet eyes. These lily-white lips, this cherry-red nose, these yellow-as-a-buttercup cheeks — they're gone, they're gone! Lovers, weep and mourn! His eyes were as green as leeks. Oh, you three Fates, come to me with your hands as pale as milk. Lay them in blood, since you have cut his thread of silk with your shears. Tongue, not a word. Come, trusty sword. Come, blade, and stab my breast! And farewell, friends. This is how Thisbe ends. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye!
[Dies.]
THESEUS. Moonshine and Lion are left to bury the dead.
DEMETRIUS. Yes, and Wall too.
BOTTOM. No, I assure you — the wall is down that separated their fathers. Would you like to see the epilogue, or would you prefer to watch a country dance performed by two of our company?

THESEUS. No epilogue, please. Your play needs no excuse. Never apologize — when all the actors are dead, there's nobody left to blame. Honestly, if the author had played Pyramus and hanged himself with Thisbe's garter, it would have been a fine tragedy. And truly, it was a fine tragedy — and very impressively performed. But come, give us your country dance. Forget the epilogue.
[Here a dance of Clowns.]

THESEUS. The iron tongue of midnight has struck twelve. Off to bed, lovers — it's nearly fairy time. I'm afraid we'll oversleep tomorrow morning as much as we've stayed up late tonight. This wonderfully crude play has helped pass the heavy hours of night quite well. Sweet friends, to bed! We'll keep this celebration going for two weeks with nightly festivities and fresh joy.
[Exeunt.]
[Enter Puck.]

PUCK. Now the hungry lion roars, and the wolf howls at the moon. The exhausted farmer snores, worn out from a long day's work. Now the dying embers glow, while the screeching owl, shrieking loudly, reminds the miserable person lying awake of death and burial shrouds. Now it is the time of night when every grave gapes wide open, and each one releases its ghost to glide along the paths near the church. And we fairies, who run alongside the moon goddess's team, following darkness like a dream — now we're playful and free. Not a mouse shall disturb this sacred house. I've been sent ahead with a broom to sweep the dust away from behind the door.
[Enter Oberon and Titania with their Train.]

OBERON. Send a shimmering light through the house, past the dying, drowsy fire. Every elf and fairy spirit, hop as lightly as a bird from a branch. And after me, sing and dance this tune with nimble grace.
TITANIA. First, learn your song by heart — a warbling note for every word. Hand in hand, with fairy grace, we will sing and bless this place.
[Song and Dance.]

OBERON. Now, until the break of day, let every fairy roam through this house. We'll go to the best marriage bed, which we shall bless. And the children born there will always be fortunate. So all three couples shall always be true in their love. And the flaws of nature's hand will not mark their children — no mole, no cleft lip, no scar, no unfortunate birthmark that people despise will appear on their children. With this consecrated dew of the fields, let every fairy take its path and bless each separate room throughout this palace with sweet peace. And may the owner of this place always rest in safety. Now go — don't delay. Meet me again at break of day.
[Exeunt Oberon, Titania and Train.]

PUCK. If we actors have offended you, just think of it this way, and everything will be fine: you were only sleeping here while these visions appeared. And this weak and silly story was nothing more than a dream. Ladies and gentlemen, please don't be angry with us. If you'll forgive us, we'll do better next time. And as I am an honest Puck — if we've been lucky enough this time to escape your harsh criticism, we'll make it up to you before long. Otherwise, call Puck a liar. So, good night to all of you. Clap your hands if we're friends, and Robin will make everything right.
[Exit.]
